Paper Name & Year: Large Language Models for Mental Health Applications (2024)
Objective: To critically assess the use of LLMs in mental health for early screening, digital interventions, and clinical settings.
Methodology: Systematic review following PRISMA guidelines across five major databases (2017–2024).
Key Findings/Conclusions: LLMs effective for detecting mental health issues and providing accessible eHealth services, but risks include hallucinations and ethical gaps.
Advantages/Strengths: Provides accessible, non-judgmental support; cost-effective; supports clinicians.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Risk of inconsistent or hallucinatory content; ethical framework gaps.
Relevance to Project: Validates use of LLM as conversational partner; highlights need for safeguards and human oversight.

Paper Name & Year: Conversational Agents for Mental Health and Wellbeing (2021)
Objective: To describe potential of conversational interfaces in mental health and identify research challenges.
Methodology: Review summarizing evidence-based research on conversational agents for training, literacy, diagnosis, and therapy.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Conversational agents improve accessibility and reduce stigma but face empathy and trust challenges.
Advantages/Strengths: Cost-effective, confidential, always available, reduces stigma.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Limited theoretical models; user engagement and empathy issues.
Relevance to Project: Informs design of conversational core; identifies empathy and trust management strategies.

Paper Name & Year: Digital vs Face-to-Face Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Depression (2022)
Objective: To compare clinical effectiveness of digital versus face-to-face CBT for major depression.
Methodology: Meta-analysis of 106 studies comparing digital and face-to-face CBT.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Digital CBT comparable to traditional CBT in efficacy but lower adherence.
Advantages/Strengths: Higher accessibility and cost-effectiveness.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Lower adherence; risk of detection bias.
Relevance to Project: Supports digital CBT as therapeutic foundation; emphasizes engagement importance.

Paper Name & Year: Natural Language Processing in Mental Health Applications (2017)
Objective: To review NLP applications using non-clinical texts for mental health analysis.
Methodology: Scoping review of literature analyzing social media and diary texts.
Key Findings/Conclusions: NLP effectively infers emotions and distress but raises privacy and accuracy concerns.
Advantages/Strengths: Scalable text analysis for detecting emotional patterns.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Privacy issues; context sensitivity may affect accuracy.
Relevance to Project: Supports emotional pattern analysis feature for journal insights.

Paper Name & Year: Privacy-Preserving AI in Mental Health: A Review of Federated Learning Approaches (2025)
Objective: To explore federated learning in mental health AI as a privacy-preserving alternative.
Methodology: Review of FL architectures and privacy-enhancing techniques (DP, MPC, Homomorphic Encryption).
Key Findings/Conclusions: FL enables collaborative AI model training without sharing sensitive data.
Advantages/Strengths: Maintains data privacy; allows collective model improvement.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Communication overhead; data heterogeneity challenges.
Relevance to Project: Justifies 'Privacy First' architecture and federated learning strategy.

Paper Name & Year: FedMentor: Domain-Aware Differential Privacy for Heterogeneous Federated LLMs in Mental Health (2025)
Objective: To propose a federated fine-tuning framework (FedMentor) using LoRA and domain-aware differential privacy for mental health LLMs.
Methodology: Development and experimental evaluation on multiple mental health datasets.
Key Findings/Conclusions: FedMentor improves safety and privacy while maintaining high model utility.
Advantages/Strengths: Balances confidentiality with model performance and scalability.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Limited discussion of method’s own weaknesses.
Relevance to Project: Informs privacy-preserving fine-tuning strategy for on-device LLM.

Paper Name & Year: Ethical Considerations in Artificial Intelligence Interventions for Mental Health and Wellbeing (2024)
Objective: To synthesize key ethical issues in AI mental health interventions and propose responsible implementation practices.
Methodology: Systematic review of literature (2014–2024) using CASP for quality assessment.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Ethical considerations include privacy, consent, bias, transparency, and accountability.
Advantages/Strengths: Provides comprehensive ethical checklist for AI systems.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Potential study selection bias.
Relevance to Project: Defines ethical safeguards across privacy, bias, and consent domains.

Paper Name & Year: OpenS2S: Advancing Fully Open-Source End-to-End Empathetic Large Speech Language Model (2025)
Objective: To introduce OpenS2S, an open-source empathetic speech LLM for transparent research.
Methodology: Development of LSLM architecture with streaming speech decoder and auto dataset pipeline.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Achieves competitive empathetic performance with lower data and compute cost.
Advantages/Strengths: Low-latency, open-source, reproducible research.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Initial overfitting during training required extra tuning.
Relevance to Project: Supports empathetic voice synthesis design.

Paper Name & Year: Talk With Human-like Agents: Empathetic Dialogue Through Perceptible Acoustic Reception and Reaction (2024)
Objective: To create a multimodal empathetic dialogue system using acoustic perception and expressive synthesis.
Methodology: Three-module system integrating speech captioning, LLM generation, and multi-attribute synthesis.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Improved understanding of prosody and emotional nuance in dialogue.
Advantages/Strengths: Accurate emotional interpretation from prosody; enhances empathy in AI responses.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Complexity may cause latency or errors.
Relevance to Project: Informs emotional tone modulation for AI speech responses.

Paper Name & Year: Validation of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (2022)
Objective: To validate PHQ-9 and GAD-7 screening tools among university students.
Methodology: Web-based survey with psychometric analysis and diagnostic interviews.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Both scales reliable; limited standalone diagnostic power.
Advantages/Strengths: Reliable tools for initial screening.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Low specificity; timing gaps in validation.
Relevance to Project: Supports inclusion of PHQ-9 and GAD-7 screening tools with disclaimers.

Paper Name & Year: User Engagement in Mobile Apps for People with Schizophrenia (2023)
Objective: To identify engagement strategies for mobile health apps targeting serious mental illness.
Methodology: Scoping review following Arksey & O’Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Effective engagement strategies include personalization, gamification, and reminders.
Advantages/Strengths: Comprehensive synthesis of engagement methods.
Disadvantages/Limitations: High heterogeneity in engagement measurement.
Relevance to Project: Provides evidence-based engagement tactics to reduce attrition.

Paper Name & Year: The Engagement Problem in Digital Mental Health Interventions (2023)
Objective: To analyze engagement challenges in DMHIs and propose strategies for improvement.
Methodology: Narrative review of patient-, intervention-, and system-level factors.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Engagement often low; human support and personalization are key drivers.
Advantages/Strengths: Identifies multi-level factors influencing adherence.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Variability across populations and app types.
Relevance to Project: Highlights need for built-in accountability mechanisms.

Paper Name & Year: Early Detection of Mental Health Crises Through AI-Powered Social Media Analysis (2024)
Objective: To explore AI use for early crisis detection from social media data.
Methodology: Multimodal deep learning model analyzing 996k social media posts validated against psychiatric assessments.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Model detects crises with 89.3% accuracy and 7.2-day lead time.
Advantages/Strengths: High accuracy and scalability across platforms.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Public data bias and ethical concerns.
Relevance to Project: Validates feasibility of crisis detection feature.

Paper Name & Year: Privacy by Design in Mobile Health (2023)
Objective: To evaluate privacy-preserving architectures in mobile health systems.
Methodology: Comparative analysis of encryption and local computation frameworks.
Key Findings/Conclusions: On-device computation enhances data protection and compliance.
Advantages/Strengths: Ensures confidentiality and security.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Computational limits on mobile devices.
Relevance to Project: Reinforces design of on-device NLP processing.

Paper Name & Year: Bias and Fairness in Mental Health AI (2024)
Objective: To examine sources of algorithmic bias in mental health AI tools.
Methodology: Review of datasets and fairness metrics for bias mitigation.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Bias in data can propagate inequities; mitigation requires diverse datasets.
Advantages/Strengths: Establishes fairness metrics and mitigation methods.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Limited empirical validation of mitigation efficacy.
Relevance to Project: Guides fairness checks for model training.

Paper Name & Year: Federated Learning for Sensitive Data (2024)
Objective: To assess the use of FL for privacy-preserving data collaboration.
Methodology: Case studies across healthcare and financial sectors.
Key Findings/Conclusions: FL maintains privacy while enabling cross-institutional learning.
Advantages/Strengths: Enables secure collaboration without data exchange.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Requires robust network synchronization.
Relevance to Project: Supports federated framework in privacy-first design.

Paper Name & Year: Differential Privacy in Healthcare AI (2024)
Objective: To evaluate DP methods for protecting sensitive patient data in AI training.
Methodology: Experimental analysis of DP noise effects on model performance.
Key Findings/Conclusions: DP protects data without major performance degradation.
Advantages/Strengths: Strong theoretical guarantees of privacy.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Can reduce model accuracy if noise excessive.
Relevance to Project: Supports privacy layer in federated model training.

Paper Name & Year: Randomized Trial of a Generative AI Chatbot for Mental Health (2025)
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a fully generative AI chatbot as an intervention for individuals with clinical-level mental health symptoms.
Methodology: Randomized controlled trial comparing chatbot intervention to waitlist control with standardized symptom scales and qualitative follow-up interviews.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Participants using the generative AI chatbot showed significant reductions in depression and anxiety scores relative to controls; adverse events were rare and mild.
Advantages/Strengths: Provides first rigorous clinical evidence of symptom improvement; highlights feasibility of AI-delivered therapy in controlled conditions.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Short study duration (4 weeks); lacks long-term follow-up and therapist comparison arm.
Relevance to Project: Validates clinical utility of LLM-based interventions; informs risk management and evaluation design for AI wellness companion.

Paper Name & Year: Combining Artificial Users and Psychotherapist Assessment to Evaluate LLM-based Mental Health Chatbots (2025)
Objective: To develop an evaluation pipeline combining artificial user simulations with expert psychotherapist scoring to assess chatbot therapeutic quality and safety.
Methodology: Hybrid evaluation using simulated user prompts representing diverse psychological profiles, analyzed by licensed clinicians for empathy, appropriateness, and safety.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Hybrid evaluation approach correlates strongly with real-user outcomes while minimizing ethical risks of testing on vulnerable populations.
Advantages/Strengths: Scalable, reproducible, and safe testing framework; integrates professional judgment into LLM evaluation loop.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Simulation fidelity limited by synthetic data realism; requires expert raters for final validation.
Relevance to Project: Provides a blueprint for evaluating AI companion’s conversational safety and therapeutic appropriateness without exposing real users to risk.

Paper Name & Year: Technological Folie à Deux: Feedback Loops Between AI Chatbots and Mental Illness (2025)
Objective: To analyze emerging bidirectional risks in interactions between emotionally adaptive chatbots and users with mental illness, focusing on co-amplification of maladaptive thoughts.
Methodology: Conceptual synthesis of clinical case reports, psychological theory, and AI alignment literature examining self-reinforcing conversational feedback loops.
Key Findings/Conclusions: Highlights risk of pathological mutual reinforcement between users and AI; calls for continuous alignment monitoring and crisis-aware dialogue modeling.
Advantages/Strengths: Identifies novel risk dimension beyond accuracy or bias; bridges psychiatry and AI safety research.
Disadvantages/Limitations: Primarily theoretical; lacks quantitative validation or empirical dataset.
Relevance to Project: Informs safety framework by anticipating dynamic feedback risks and promoting adaptive supervision in AI-based wellness companions.
